Mapping In navigation applications, grid maps are used to represent the oc - cupancy status of different locations in the world. In grid maps, the space is discretized into cells to approximate the obstacles in the real world, and each grid stores the probability that the cell is occupied by an obstacle. Given the crop row detection results, a local 2D grid map representing the crop row locations was constructed in real-time. The grid map was pie-shaped, with a radius of 2.5 m, which is consistent with the sensor ’ s field of view ( Fig. 8 a). The cell size was set to 2.5 cm based on the concerns of navigation accuracy requirement, the sensor accuracy, and the computational cost. Based on the beam model of range finders theory ( Thrun et al., 2005 ), the cells in the local map were divided into three categories: free space, occupied space, and unknown space, with occupancy probability of 0.3, 0.7 and 0.5, respectively. The categorization is performed according to the detected crop row position. Based on the available global pose of the robot, the local map was used to update the global occupancy map ( Fig. 8 b). In PhenoBot 3.0, various sensors were used to accomplish the navi - gation task, including a ToF camera, an RTK-GPS module, two Inertia measurement units (IMU), and a set of encoders. The main sensor for vision-based navigation functions is a StarForm Swift-G ToF camera (Odos Imaging, Scotland). The camera equips with seven strong infrared LED light sources, which enables the camera to operate in outdoor conditions. It has view angles of 43 ◦ x 33 ◦ , and outputs depth and infrared intensity images simultaneously with a resolution of 640 × 480. The precision of depth measurement is in centimeter-level when oper - ating at the range of 0.3 m-2.5 m, which is sufficient for crop row detection. This reported research was set out to investigate the feasibility of using a front-facing Time-of-Flight (ToF) camera to detect crop rows for navigation under the canopy of crops with narrow row spacing, such as corn and sorghum. The specific objectives were to (1) assess the devel - oped under-canopy ToF-camera-based crop row detection algorithm; (2) evaluate the mapping and inter-row vehicle localization performance using the proposed row-detection algorithm. This paper is organized as follows: In section 2, our developed robot PhenoBot 3.0 as the experimental platform is introduced, and the pipeline of crop row detection, inter-row vehicle localization and map generation is described.
